questions.question: You are designing a globally distributed social media feed service. During a temporary network partition between regions, product insists that users must still be able to post and read most recent content without errors. Which CAP choice BEST matches this requirement for the write path?

options.text: Prioritize Consistency and Partition Tolerance (CP), reject writes during partition to avoid divergence
Prioritize Availability and Partition Tolerance (AP), accept writes in each partition and reconcile later
Prioritize Consistency and Availability (CA), rely on synchronous replication across all regions
Ignore CAP and rely only on horizontal scaling of a single-region database

questions.explanation: During a network partition, you cannot simultaneously guarantee both strict consistency and availability. If product insists that users can continue reading and writing without errors, you are prioritizing availability under partitions. This aligns with an AP choice: accept writes in each partition and handle conflicts or reconciliation later. CP (A) would reject or block writes to maintain consistency, violating the requirement. CA (C) is not achievable under partitions because synchronous replication would fail when the network is split. D ignores the partition scenario altogether and conflicts with global distribution requirements.

questions.question: A read-heavy analytics dashboard must show near-real-time metrics but can tolerate slightly stale data (a few seconds delay). Which combination of design choices is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Single strongly consistent relational database with all reads and writes going to the primary instance
Leader-follower database with followers serving reads and asynchronous replication from the leader
Sharded database where each shard is strongly consistent and all reads go to the shard leaders only
In-memory cache in front of a single-node database with cache write-through on every update

questions.explanation: For a read-heavy workload that can tolerate slightly stale data, leader-follower (primary-replica) with asynchronous replication is a natural fit. Followers scale out read traffic while allowing some replication lag, which the requirement tolerates. A bottlenecks all reads on the primary and may not scale well. C still forces all reads to leaders, which limits read scaling and mainly helps with data volume, not read fanout. D adds a cache but keeps a single-node database as a write bottleneck and does not inherently provide horizontal read scaling across replicas like B.

questions.question: You are designing an API rate limiter for a large multi-tenant SaaS platform. Which design choice MOST improves both scalability and fairness across tenants?

options.text: Use a local in-process counter per API node without any shared state
Use a global distributed counter in a strongly consistent database table
Use a token bucket per tenant stored in a distributed in-memory key-value store (e.g., Redis), with keys sharded by tenant ID
Use a fixed global QPS limit stored in a configuration file and shared across all tenants

questions.explanation: A token bucket per tenant stored in a distributed in-memory store allows you to enforce per-tenant limits fairly while scaling horizontally: keys can be sharded by tenant ID across multiple nodes. Local in-process counters (A) break when traffic is distributed across many API nodes and cannot enforce a global limit. A single strongly consistent counter (B) will quickly become a hot spot and a bottleneck. A fixed global QPS limit (D) cannot ensure fairness across tenants and is too coarse-grained for a multi-tenant system.

questions.question: You are designing an image sharing service where users frequently read their own recent photos and occasionally older photos. Storage is in an object store (like S3). Which caching strategy MOST effectively reduces median and tail read latency while keeping invalidation manageable?

options.text: No cache at all; always read directly from object storage
Global write-through cache where every image write goes to cache and storage, and all reads go to cache first
Read-through cache with LRU eviction, where cache entries are populated on read and evicted based on recency
Full preloading cache where all user images are cached permanently regardless of access patterns

questions.explanation: A read-through cache with LRU eviction automatically caches frequently accessed items (like recent photos) and evicts cold items, which matches the access pattern. This reduces median and tail latency while keeping cache size under control without complex invalidation logic. A offers no latency benefits. B adds complexity and can waste cache space on rarely-read images; it also requires writing to the cache on every upload. D is unrealistic at scale because it attempts to cache everything and will exceed memory constraints or lead to constant thrashing.

questions.question: You are designing a high-write leaderboard service for a mobile game. Players submit score updates frequently, and you must show the top N scores globally with low latency. Which storage and indexing approach is MOST suitable?

options.text: Append-only log file on disk that is periodically sorted offline to recompute the leaderboard
Relational database table with a B-tree index on the score column and full table scans for top N queries
In-memory sorted set data structure (e.g., Redis sorted set) keyed by leaderboard, with scores as the sort key
Document database with each player document containing an array of all historical scores

questions.explanation: An in-memory sorted set (like Redis ZSET) is designed for exactly this pattern: frequent updates and fast top N queries by score. It provides O(log n) inserts and efficient range queries. A introduces high latency and staleness because the leaderboard is only updated after offline processing. B can handle this for smaller scales but top N queries will stress the database and index; under very high write rates, it becomes a bottleneck. D forces you to read and aggregate arrays of scores per user, which is inefficient and poorly suited for global ranking queries.

questions.question: You are designing a notification service that must deliver push notifications to millions of devices. Notifications can arrive in bursts, but slight delivery delay (seconds) is acceptable. Which architecture choice BEST handles bursty traffic while keeping the core service resilient?

options.text: Have the web/API tier synchronously call the push provider (e.g., FCM/APNS) for each notification request
Place a durable message queue between the producer and multiple notification worker services that send pushes
Write notifications directly into a relational database and have clients poll periodically for new rows
Use a single cron job that runs every minute and sends all pending notifications in a tight loop

questions.explanation: A durable message queue decouples producers from consumers and naturally absorbs bursts: producers can enqueue messages quickly while workers scale horizontally to process the queue and talk to push providers. A makes the API tier directly dependent on push provider latency and failures. C forces clients into inefficient polling and puts unnecessary load on the database. D introduces a coarse time granularity and single point of failure that cannot react smoothly to burst patterns.

questions.question: You are designing a multi-region read API for a product catalog. Data is mastered in a single primary region but must be served with low latency globally. Strong consistency on reads is NOT required, but reads should be fast and mostly fresh. Which approach is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Serve all reads from the primary region and rely on aggressive HTTP caching headers at the client side only
Replicate data asynchronously to read replicas in each region and route users to their nearest replica
Use a synchronous two-phase commit across all regions for every write before allowing any read
Write data independently in every region and run an eventual reconciliation job nightly

questions.explanation: Asynchronous replication to regional read replicas gives low-latency local reads with acceptable staleness, which matches the requirement. A will have high latency for distant users. C greatly increases write latency and availability issues due to the need for cross-region coordination on every write. D allows large divergence (full-day discrepancies) and complex conflict resolution that is excessive for a product catalog that only needs mostly fresh, not region-siloed, data.

questions.question: You are designing a logging system that ingests logs from thousands of microservices and supports near-real-time search and alerting. Which combination of components is MOST suitable?

options.text: Services write logs to local files; operators manually copy and grep them on demand
Services send logs to a central message bus (e.g., Kafka), then a log processor indexes them into a search engine (e.g., Elasticsearch)
Services directly write logs into a relational database table, and alerts run as SQL queries
Services send logs via email to a shared inbox that SREs monitor

questions.explanation: Streaming logs into a central message bus and then indexing them into a search engine is the standard pattern for scalable, near-real-time logging and alerting. Kafka (or similar) buffers spikes, and Elasticsearch (or similar) enables fast queries and aggregations. A is purely manual and unscalable. C will overload the relational database with high write volume and large unstructured payloads. D is clearly not viable for any serious scale or automated alerting.

questions.question: You are designing an API that needs to ensure idempotent processing of payment requests so that retried requests (due to client or network timeouts) do not result in duplicate charges. Which approach MOST directly ensures idempotency at the application level?

options.text: Rely on the HTTP POST verb semantics and trust clients not to resend requests
Require clients to send a unique idempotency key per logical payment, and deduplicate requests on the server using this key
Use only HTTP GET for payment requests so that intermediate caches can safely retry
Log every request and manually inspect logs for duplicates

questions.explanation: An idempotency key uniquely identifies a logical operation (e.g., charge this card for this order). The server can store the result for each key and return the same result on retries, preventing duplicate charges. A is unsafe because POST semantics do not enforce idempotency. C misuses GET, which is meant to be safe and cacheable, and is not appropriate for payments. D is manual and cannot reliably prevent duplicates at scale.

questions.question: You are designing a microservices architecture for an e-commerce platform. Which combination of characteristics MOST strongly suggests that you should maintain a monolith for now instead of aggressively splitting into many microservices?

options.text: Team size is small, deployment frequency is modest, and cross-service boundaries are unclear
Many teams own different parts of the system and frequently deploy independently
You have strict multi-language requirements and each component needs different tech stacks
You already have separate databases per bounded context and strong domain boundaries

questions.explanation: Microservices add operational complexity: network calls, distributed tracing, deployment orchestration, and cross-service failures. If your team is small, deployment cadence is moderate, and boundaries between components are not well-understood, a monolith is usually simpler and safer. B, C, and D are all signals that microservices might be justified: multiple teams and frequent deployments, heterogeneous tech requirements, or clearly separated bounded contexts with separate data stores.
